title: Voces de Resistencia Cap.1 – Cantadoras de Pogue
note: Documentary segment; alabaos are Afro-Colombian funerary chants from the Pacific; the Pogue group began composing new alabaos after the 2002 Bojayá massacre to honor victims and demand justice, turning the tradition into a form of political memory and resistance

title: Alabao
note: Elena Hinestroza, known as 'la Cantadora de la Paz,' is from Timbiquí, Cauca; displaced by armed conflict in 2008, she now leads the group Integración Pacífica from Cali and uses song, including alabaos, as a tool for healing and community leadership

title: En los Manglares
note: Official video; Góngora, from Timbiquí, Cauca, describes it as an 'alabao beat,' a song for remembrance inspired by funerary ritual tradition, reworked with contemporary production

title: Colombia Tierra Querida
note: Live performance (recovered/digitized recording, likely 1980's), sung by Orlando Quesada with Lucho Bermúdez's orchestra; widely regarded as a 'second national anthem'; Bermúdez adapted traditional cumbia and porro into big-band orchestral arrangements starting in the 1930's, shaping modern Colombian musical identity

title: Limpia Bambarita
note: Live performance at Festival Raíces Bogotá Andina 2021; features Andrea Echeverri singing in Inga/Quechua; from the album Surestar; Bambarabanda blends Andean melodies with rock and theatrical elements

title: Hoy Para Siempre
artist: Los Rolling Ruanas ft. Catalina García
note: Live performance – 2017 (the official video, shot at Laguna Verde, Volcán Azufral, Nariño, isn't embeddable); the band is based in Bogotá but its members have family roots in Boyacá (Tibasosa, Oicatá, Paipa, Duitama) and Vélez; they paired campesino instrumentation (tiple, guacharaca) with rock, inspired by sonsureño sounds of the Nariño/Ecuador border, as a tribute to the Pachamama

title: Caminito de piedra
note: Official video; first single from the EP Sembrando canciones pa' hacer crecer la vida; Bogotá-based group inspired by páramo/highland traditional music connecting Cauca, Boyacá, and Santander

title: Tequendama
note: Live performance – March 2021, Basílica Menor del Voto Nacional, Bogotá; Moque blends Andean ancestral traditions (e.g. Fandango del Imbabura, Bambuco cundiboyacense) described as a reencounter with living memory rather than a modernizing fusion

title: Kaipimikanchi
note: From their self-titled 2019 album; formed in Pasto in 2015; recreates communal festival music (raymis, sanjuanitos) of ancestral peoples of southern Nariño and northern Ecuador, blending ancestral sound with a contemporary approach; the name is Quechua for 'here we are'

title: Qué vo' hacer
note: Live performance – 2012 (Señal Radiónica); first single from the album Tripping Tropicana; reached #1 on Colombian rock charts and earned the band a Latin Grammy nomination; blends rock with salsa, boogaloo, and Caribbean rhythms

title: Cortejo Fúnebre
note: Live performance at Destroying Fest, Houston, Texas – July 1, 2022; track from the album Reqviem; pioneering Colombian death metal band formed in Medellín in 1988, with lyrics reflecting the violence of that era

title: Deja
note: Official video, released 2003 on the album 3AM (In Beats We Trust); Sidestepper, founded by British producer Richard Blair with Iván Benavides, pioneered Colombian 'electro-cumbia' by fusing Afro-Colombian rhythms with drum and bass and dub

title: Jardín Secreto
note: Live acoustic ('desconectado') session for Amplificado.tv, 2013; Bogotá quartet inspired by Django Reinhardt's gypsy jazz tradition, one of the few Colombian bands in this genre

title: Ojos Verdes
note: Live on KEXP, recorded April 1, 2024; Bogotá trio (formed 2020) blending cumbia, surf rock, funk, and Turkish musical influences

title: Fuego
note: Live performance for KEXP, 2009; from the 2008 album Estalla, the song that first established the band internationally; vocalist Li Saumet was born in Santa Marta, and the band's Caribbean/tropical sound is rooted in her coast even though it formed in Bogotá

title: Fiesta Candelaria
note: Live performance at Música en el Parque, Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, 2022; title track of the band's 2025 album, released for their 25th anniversary; Puerto Candelaria, formed in Medellín in 2000, blends cumbia, porro, jazz, ska, and Latin pop with reflection and celebration

title: La Nevera
note: Live performance – 1st Festival de la Tigra, Piedecuesta, 2017; originally a solo voice-and-guitar track from Edson Velandia's 2015 album El Karateka, reworked into a rockier band version; 'rasqa' is a genre coined by the band, fusing Andean folk rhythms with punk and heavy rock attitude; the festival was founded by band members Edson Velandia and Adriana Lizcano

title: El Alma y el Cuerpo
note: Live performance for KEXP, recorded April 3, 2013; first single from the 2012 album Elegancia Tropical, one of the more introspective tracks in the band's catalogue; vocalist Li Saumet was born in Santa Marta, and the band's Caribbean/tropical sound is rooted in her coast even though it formed in Bogotá
